subtype: Approach: sharing pet duties fairly among siblings [Action]
passage: Children, you're fighting again over whose turn it is with the parrot? Sit. When I was a girl of ten and my sister Zohra was eight, our Abba brought home a hamster in a shoebox. For one whole week we quarrelled every day. "I fed him yesterday!" "No, I did!" Once he got fed twice, and once not at all. So Ammi hung a calendar next to the cage and gave us two pencils, red for me, green for Zohra. Odd dates were mine, even dates were hers. Food, fresh water, and clean the corner of the cage. When you finished, you put your colour on the date. After that, if anyone said "your turn", we just looked at the calendar. I, Farida, cannot remember one more fight about that hamster.

qa.q: Which colour pencil was Zohra's?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: How did young Farida feel during the week of quarrels?
qa.a: Farida felt cross and frustrated, sure of having fed the hamster when Zohra said otherwise.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story ended the quarrels?
qa.a: Ammi's calendar with odd and even dates and a coloured mark for each job, because it made every turn visible.

qa.q: What was that first week like for the hamster?
qa.a: Unsettled: it was fed twice on one day and not at all on another.

grounding: An elder recalls two sisters taking alternate days to feed and clean a hamster and marking a calendar, which ended their arguments.

subtype: Approach: sharing pet duties fairly among siblings [Action]
passage: Kavitha and her younger sister Harini had shared Pista the hamster since March, and it had been one long argument. Then Kavitha had an idea: alternate days, marked on the kitchen calendar. K on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays; H on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays; Sundays together. It worked for a month. Then Harini left for a five-day school camp, Monday to Friday. "Who does my days?" she wailed at the door. Kavitha looked at the calendar. "I'll do them. You take the same number of mine when you're back." She crossed out the two H's that week and wrote K beside each, so there'd be no argument later. When Harini got home, she looked at the calendar, counted, and without being asked did Kavitha's next two days.

qa.q: Which days were Harini's?
qa.a: Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

qa.q: What was Harini feeling at the door?
qa.a: Anxious about who would look after Pista on her days while she was away.

qa.q: What else could the sisters arrange for a longer trip?
qa.a: They could ask a parent to cover some days, so the whole load does not fall on one sister.

qa.q: How does the calendar help Kavitha?
qa.a: Kavitha can see exactly how many days she covered, so she is paid back fairly without a quarrel.

grounding: Two sisters share hamster care on alternate days marked on a calendar, which keeps things fair even when one goes away.

subtype: Approach: short daily practice at a fixed time [Action]
passage: For three weeks Rashmi had meant to practise the harmonium "sometime in the evening", and most evenings sometime never came. Homework ran late, or Gargi from the next flat called her down to play. So on Sunday she agreed a plan with her mother: fifteen minutes, straight after the evening snack, before anything else. On Monday she put her empty glass in the sink, opened the harmonium on the divan and set the kitchen timer. Sa re ga ma, then the first line of the bhajan. When the timer rang, she stopped. On Wednesday Gargi called up from the courtyard. "Ten minutes!" Rashmi shouted back, not stopping. By the second week her fingers found the keys without her thinking, and the snack itself had become the signal.

qa.q: How long does Rashmi practise each day?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes.

qa.q: How does practice feel to Rashmi by the second week?
qa.a: It feels easier and more natural; she seems relieved that she no longer has to decide when to play.

qa.q: What else could help on days when snack time is disturbed?
qa.a: A second fixed slot, such as right after dinner, so a busy day does not mean no practice.

qa.q: How might Gargi see the new routine?
qa.a: Gargi has to wait a few minutes, but can count on Rashmi coming down once practice is over.

grounding: A girl practises harmonium for fifteen minutes straight after her evening snack, and the fixed time makes practice easier.

subtype: Approach: short daily practice at a fixed time [Action]
passage:
"Sharmila, come down, we're playing langdi!"
"In fifteen minutes, Ankita."
"You always say that now. What are you doing?"
"Harmonium. Right after my snack. Every day."
"Why after snack? Why not later?"
"Because 'later' never came. Last month I practised maybe twice a week. I'd think, after homework, after TV, after dinner. Then I'd be sleepy."
"And now?"
"Now I eat my poha, wash my hands, sit. I don't even have to decide. My teacher noticed on Saturday. She said my left hand is steadier."
"Fifteen minutes exactly?"
"Timer's on. Eleven left. Go and start without me."
"No way. We'll wait. But be quick."

qa.q: What does Sharmila eat before practising?
qa.a: Poha.

qa.q: How does Sharmila seem to feel about the new routine?
qa.a: Relieved not to have to decide each day, and quietly proud that her teacher noticed a steadier left hand.

qa.q: What else could Sharmila try if friends keep calling during practice?
qa.a: Tell her friends her practice time in advance, so they plan the game to start after it.

qa.q: How does Ankita respond to the routine?
qa.a: Ankita is impatient at first, then chooses to wait for Sharmila. 😊

grounding: A girl explains how practising straight after her evening snack made harmonium practice easier than choosing a time each day.

subtype: Approach: breaking a song into small parts [Thinking]
passage: In the back room of his uncle's tailoring shop, in a small town near Lucknow, Rafiq sat with the old tabla his grandfather had played. The kaida his teacher, Zubin-ustad, had set was sixteen beats long, and every time Rafiq tried the whole thing, his fingers tangled by the fifth beat. He put his hands in his lap and thought. "Dha dha. I can do dha dha. Anyone can do dha dha." He played just those two, very slowly, ten times. Then the next two: ti ta. Then all four together. "It's not one big hard thing," he muttered. "It's eight small easy things holding hands." By the time the sewing machines went quiet for evening prayers, he had twelve beats joined up.

qa.q: How many beats long was the kaida?
qa.a: Sixteen beats.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel before he put his hands in his lap?
qa.a: Frustrated, because his fingers kept tangling by the fifth beat.

qa.q: What else could Rafiq do with the last four beats tomorrow?
qa.a: Warm up with the twelve he has, then add the last pairs slowly, the same way, before trying the full speed.

qa.q: What would change if Rafiq kept playing all sixteen beats at full speed?
qa.a: His fingers would likely keep tangling at the fifth beat, and he would stay stuck and frustrated.

grounding: A boy stuck on a tabla piece practises it two beats at a time, reasoning that a hard piece is many small ones joined.

subtype: Approach: breaking a song into small parts [Thinking]
passage: Pablo was the only kid at his Madrid music school who had picked the tabla, and on Thursday he had to play the new composition for the class. The middle went fast, a flurry of strokes his teacher made sound like rain. Pablo's fingers turned it into a mess every time. On Tuesday evening his sister Layla found him on the floor with a pencil, drawing lines between the syllables on the sheet. "What are you doing?" "Cutting it up," he said. "Look: this bit is just two strokes. I can do two strokes. And this bit is two more." He played the first pair slowly, then the second, then joined them. Then the third pair. By Thursday his rain was slower than his teacher's, but every drop was there.

qa.q: When did Pablo have to play for the class?
qa.a: On Thursday.

qa.q: What was Pablo thinking as he drew lines on the sheet?
qa.a: He felt determined and hopeful, seeing the hard part as small pairs he could manage.

qa.q: What else could Pablo try once all the pieces join?
qa.a: Raise the speed a little each day, so the rain gets faster without the strokes falling apart.

qa.q: How might Layla see the pencil lines at first?
qa.a: Layla seems curious and a bit puzzled, until Pablo explains he is cutting the piece up.

grounding: A boy breaks a fast tabla passage into pairs of strokes, practising each slowly before joining them.

subtype: Approach: playing only the parts already known [Pitfall]
passage: Every evening in their Noida flat, Payal sat at the keyboard and played the opening of the river song, eight bars she could manage with her eyes closed. It sounded lovely. Her little brother Eshaan even danced to it. Then came the middle, where the left hand jumped, and Payal's fingers stumbled. She'd stop, go back to the start and play the lovely bit again. Every Saturday her teacher listened, nodded at the opening, and at the middle said, "Same place as last week." For five Saturdays it was the same place. On the sixth, a student who had started after Payal played the river song, straight through the middle. Payal stared at her own hands.

qa.q: How many bars could Payal play with her eyes closed?
qa.a: Eight bars.

qa.q: What might Payal be feeling as she stares at her hands?
qa.a: Embarrassed and frustrated, realising she has been stuck in the same place for weeks.

qa.q: What else could Payal try in her practice?
qa.a: Start each practice with the difficult middle, slowly, and save the easy opening as a reward at the end.

qa.q: What is Payal's practice like for Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan only hears the lovely opening and dances to it, so he has no idea the middle is stuck.

grounding: A child keeps replaying the easy opening of a song, so the hard middle never improves and each lesson feels the same.

subtype: Approach: playing only the parts already known [Pitfall]
passage:
"Lovely intro, Anirban. Now from the chorus, please."
"Can I do the intro once more first, Miss Elizabeth?"
"You've played it four times today."
"It sounds good, though."
"It does. It sounded good last week too. And the week before. What about the chorus?"
"The chorus is... I've been getting to it."
"How often did you practise the chorus at home?"
Anirban looked at his shoes. "I start from the top every time. By the time I get to the chorus, I'm tired."
"So the intro gets thirty turns and the chorus gets none."
"...Yes."
"And that's why today feels exactly like last Tuesday."
"It does feel the same." He sighed. "Boring, actually."

qa.q: How many times had Anirban played the intro today?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What does Anirban looking at his shoes suggest?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, knowing he had been avoiding the chorus.

qa.q: What else could Anirban try at home?
qa.a: Begin each practice with the chorus while he is fresh, and play the intro only afterwards.

qa.q: How does Miss Elizabeth see the pattern?
qa.a: Miss Elizabeth sees clearly that the intro gets all the practice and the chorus none, and says so patiently but directly.

grounding: A boy keeps playing the easy intro he knows, so the chorus never improves and each lesson feels the same.

subtype: Approach: using a teacher's feedback to correct errors [Revision]
passage: At the music centre in Aizawl, Ritu-ma'am stopped Lalremsiami halfway through the song. "Your G chord sounds like it's under a blanket. Look at your third finger. It's lying on the next string." Lalremsiami felt her cheeks go hot. She had been playing that chord muffled for a month without noticing. After class she didn't leave. She took her guitar to the practice room with the long mirror and sat facing it. She placed her fingers slowly, one at a time, watching the third finger stand up on its tip. Strum. Clear. Again, slower. Clear. She played the change from C to G twenty times, checking the mirror each time. On Friday Ritu-ma'am listened to the whole song and simply nodded.

qa.q: Which chord sounded muffled?
qa.a: The G chord.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel when the teacher pointed out the chord?
qa.a: Embarrassed, with her cheeks going hot, since she had not noticed for a month.

qa.q: What else could she do to keep the chord right at home?
qa.a: Prop up a small mirror or watch her hand while practising slowly, so the finger habit sticks.

qa.q: How might Ritu-ma'am see the change on Friday?
qa.a: Ritu-ma'am simply nodded, which suggests satisfaction that the correction had been used.

grounding: A girl uses her guitar teacher's feedback, slowing down and watching her hand in a mirror to fix a muffled chord.

subtype: Approach: using a teacher's feedback to correct errors [Revision]
passage: I'm Eshaan, Vidya's brother. For weeks her guitar made one ugly buzzing sound in the middle of every song. On Saturday her teacher wrote something in her notebook, and Vidya came home quiet. That evening she carried Mummy's dressing-table mirror into her room, leaned it against the cupboard and sat in front of it. I watched from the doorway. She played the same chord again and again, very slowly, looking at the mirror, then at her hand, then back. Once she moved a finger closer to the metal bar. The buzz stopped. She played it ten more times, still slowly. Now the song has no buzz. I asked what the teacher had written. She said, "Fingertips, not flat fingers." She didn't look upset any more.

qa.q: What had the teacher written, according to Vidya?
qa.a: "Fingertips, not flat fingers."

qa.q: What might Vidya have felt when she came home on Saturday?
qa.a: She seemed quiet, perhaps discouraged or upset by the correction.

qa.q: What else could Vidya try if the buzz comes back?
qa.a: Slow down again in front of the mirror, and ask her teacher to check her hand at the next lesson.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see the change?
qa.a: Eshaan notices the buzz has gone and that Vidya no longer looks upset.

grounding: A brother watches a girl use her teacher's note and a mirror to correct her finger position and fix a buzzing chord.

subtype: Approach: rushing to play fast [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Charu, Shankar's cousin, and I was at Dadi's birthday dinner when he played. Everyone asked for the keyboard piece he'd been learning. He grinned, cracked his knuckles and went at it like a train. It was fast, I'll give him that. But there were wrong notes in almost every line, and he played the same one wrong three times, as if his fingers had learnt it that way. Everyone clapped anyway. Dadi said, "So fast!" The next Saturday I went with him to his lesson. His teacher listened for ten seconds, stopped him and switched on a metronome. It went tick... tick... tick, very slowly. "At this speed, please. Every note right." Shankar's face went red. I don't know if he was angry or embarrassed.

qa.q: What did Dadi say after the performance?
qa.a: "So fast!"

qa.q: Why did Shankar play so fast at the dinner?
qa.a: He was excited and eager to impress the family, wanting the speed to wow them.

qa.q: What else could Shankar do before performing next time?
qa.a: Practise slowly with the metronome until each note is right, then raise the speed bit by bit.

qa.q: How does Charu read Shankar's red face?
qa.a: Charu cannot tell whether it shows anger or embarrassment.

grounding: A cousin watches a boy race through a keyboard piece to impress the family, building mistakes his teacher corrects with a slow metronome.

subtype: Approach: rushing to play fast [Pitfall]
passage:
Sunday: On the family video call, Raghav played his keyboard piece for Nani and his cousins at double speed. Notes crashed into each other. His sister Ankita winced, but Nani clapped. "What speed!"
Tuesday: At his lesson Raghav raced again. His teacher let him finish, then pointed at the page. "Bar six: you played B instead of C. Every time. Your fingers have learnt the mistake." The teacher set the metronome to a slow tick and wrote the setting on the page. "This speed until Friday."
Friday: Raghav sat through the slow ticks every evening, jaw tight at first. By Friday bar six came out C every time, and when Ankita walked past she said, "Oh. That's what it's supposed to sound like."

qa.q: Which wrong note did Raghav keep playing in bar six?
qa.a: B instead of C.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel sitting through the slow ticks at first?
qa.a: Impatient and frustrated, with his jaw tight.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Raghav practises?
qa.a: Play slowly with the metronome every day and speed up only once each bar is right.

qa.q: How does Ankita's reaction change?
qa.a: Ankita winced on Sunday; by Friday she is surprised and pleased to hear how it should sound.

grounding: Across a week, a boy who rushed a keyboard piece to impress family is set a slow metronome and fixes his wrong note.

subtype: Approach: setting a goal for a school concert [Thinking]
passage:
Monday
Annual Day is six weeks from today, and Reena-ma'am says I can play the school song on the keyboard. I sat on my bed and counted backwards. Week six is the show. Weeks five and six should be for polishing and for playing it to Ammi and Abbu and even our grumpy neighbour uncle, so I get used to people watching. That means I must know every note by the end of week four. The song has four parts. So: one part each week, weeks one to four. This week is part one. It feels much less scary written down like this. I stuck the plan inside my music file.
Parveen

qa.q: How many weeks away is Annual Day?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: How does Parveen feel after writing the plan?
qa.a: Parveen feels much less scared, calmer now that the weeks are laid out.

qa.q: What else could Parveen do if one part turns out harder?
qa.a: Parveen could give that part extra practice each day or start it early, so week four still holds.

qa.q: How might Ammi and Abbu experience weeks five and six?
qa.a: They will hear the song many times and help Parveen get used to an audience, and are likely to feel proud.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child working backward from a concert date to set weekly goals for learning and polishing a song.

subtype: Approach: setting a goal for a school concert [Thinking]
passage: The notice board at the girls' school in Rampur said the Annual Function would be in six weeks. Himani had been chosen to play the harmonium for the welcome song. Walking home past the mustard fields with her friend Anjali, she thought it through out loud. "The last week is for playing it in front of people. The week before that, too. So it has to be ready by the end of week four." She counted on her fingers. "Three verses and the chorus. Four weeks. One each week." Anjali said, "What if one verse is hard?" Himani thought. "Then I do the hard one first, while there's time." That evening she wrote the weeks inside her notebook cover, with the third verse next to week one.

qa.q: What did Himani write inside her notebook cover?
qa.a: The weeks, with the third verse next to week one.

qa.q: What was Himani thinking on the walk home?
qa.a: She felt calm and determined, working backward from the function to fix what each week needed.

qa.q: What else could help Himani in the last two weeks?
qa.a: Playing for her family or Anjali each evening, so an audience feels normal by the function.

qa.q: How might Anjali see the plan?
qa.a: Anjali raised a real worry and saw Himani adjust for it, so Anjali may feel part of the plan.

grounding: A girl works backward from a school function six weeks away to decide when the song must be learnt and when to polish it.

subtype: Approach: quitting after the first difficult stage [Pitfall]
passage:
"Pradeep, where's your flute? Class is starting."
"At home. In the cupboard. I'm stopping, Tenzin."
"Stopping? It's been two weeks!"
"My lips hurt after five minutes. And every note squeaks like a door. You heard it."
"Everyone squeaks. I squeaked for a month."
"Your squeaks sounded better than mine."
"They sounded exactly the same, trust me."
"No. Some people just have talent. I don't."
"Sir said the first few weeks are the worst."
"Sir says that to everyone."
The music teacher began the scale, and eleven flutes piped up. Pradeep sat with his empty hands under the desk. By the end of term Tenzin could play the whole school song.

qa.q: How long had Pradeep been learning the flute?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What does Pradeep believe about himself, and how does he feel?
qa.a: He believes he has no talent, and he feels discouraged and embarrassed by the squeaks.

qa.q: What else could Pradeep have tried?
qa.a: Shorter practice sessions and asking the teacher about his lip position, to get through the sore, squeaky stage.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see Pradeep quitting?
qa.a: Tenzin is surprised and tries to encourage him, insisting his own squeaks sounded the same.

grounding: A boy quits the flute when his lips hurt and the notes squeak, believing he lacks talent, while his friend keeps going.

subtype: Approach: quitting after the first difficult stage [Pitfall]
passage: When I was nine, I, Bhupen, took up the bamboo flute because my cousin Kiran was learning. For the first ten days my lips went sore and numb, and every note came out as a hiss or a shriek. Kiran's notes sounded clear to me. I decided I just didn't have it, and I put the flute in the drawer under my bed. Nobody told me, and I didn't ask, that almost everyone sounds like a kettle at first. Years later Kiran told me the teacher had said it to the whole class: the first month hurts. I had missed that class. Kiran plays at weddings now. My flute is still in the drawer, and sometimes I take it out and wonder.

qa.q: Where did Bhupen put the flute?
qa.a: In the drawer under the bed.

qa.q: How does Bhupen feel now when taking the flute out?
qa.a: Wistful and a little regretful, wondering what might have been.

qa.q: What else could Bhupen have done in those first ten days?
qa.a: Ask Kiran or the teacher whether sore lips and squeaks are normal, and keep going with short practices.

qa.q: What was the first month like for Kiran?
qa.a: Kiran heard the teacher say the first month hurts, kept going through it, and now plays at weddings.

grounding: Looking back, a child describes quitting the flute during the painful beginner stage without knowing most learners go through it.

subtype: Approach: recording practice to hear mistakes [Action]
passage: Last term I was learning a sitar piece that I thought I was playing perfectly. I'm Aparna. My brother Jatin said something sounded "wobbly", but he couldn't say where. So one evening I borrowed Amma's phone, propped it on the pillow and recorded myself. Listening back was awful and useful at the same time. Every time I moved from Sa up to Ga, I slowed down, like a cycle going uphill. I hadn't heard it while playing because I was busy with my fingers. After that I practised only those two notes for three days, back and forth, counting aloud. Then I recorded again. The uphill bit had become flat road.

qa.q: Where did Aparna prop the phone?
qa.a: On the pillow.

qa.q: How did listening back feel to Aparna?
qa.a: Awful and useful at once: uncomfortable to hear, but a relief to find exactly where the problem was.

qa.q: What else could Aparna try with the recordings?
qa.a: Keep the old and new recordings to compare, or play along with a steady clap to keep the beat.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel about his 'wobbly' comment now?
qa.a: Jatin's vague comment led to the fix, so Jatin might feel useful and pleased.

grounding: Looking back, a child records practice on a parent's phone, hears the rhythm slow at a note change and works on that spot.

subtype: Approach: recording practice to hear mistakes [Action]
passage:
Music room note, Wednesday.
Pema asked last week whether she could record her violin practice at home on her mother's phone. Today she brought the recording and played it for me with a pencil in her hand. "Listen here," she said, and stopped it. "Every time I go from the A string to the E string, I drag." She was right; I had noticed it but had not yet mentioned it. She had already marked the spot on her sheet with a small star. For the rest of the lesson she played only those two bars, slowly, while I clapped the beat, and then recorded them again. The second recording was steady. I have suggested she keep one recording each week, so she can hear her own progress.
Pallavi, music teacher

qa.q: Where does Pema drag?
qa.a: Going from the A string to the E string.

qa.q: How did Pema seem to feel while sharing the recording?
qa.a: Confident and pleased, even proud, to have found the problem herself.

qa.q: What else could Pema do with a recording each week?
qa.a: Compare them over the term, so she can hear which spots have improved and which still need work.

qa.q: How does Pallavi see Pema's discovery?
qa.a: Pallavi had noticed the drag but not yet said so, and seems impressed that Pema found it on her own.

grounding: A music teacher's note records a girl using phone recordings to hear where her rhythm slows and practising that spot.

subtype: Approach: practising with a friend for motivation [Action]
passage: The practice rooms at the community music hall were free on Saturday mornings, and Sangeeta and Pranav had booked room 3, nine to ten, for the whole term. Some Saturdays Sangeeta woke up wanting to pull the blanket over her head. But she knew Pranav would already be at the gate with his violin case, and she'd feel terrible leaving him alone in there. So she went. They took turns: one played the week's piece while the other listened, then said one good thing and one thing to fix. Pranav's bow bounced; Sangeeta rushed the endings. By December neither had missed a single Saturday, and at the winter recital they played a duet.

qa.q: Which room did they book, and when?
qa.a: Room 3, from nine to ten on Saturday mornings.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta still go on lazy Saturdays, and what was she feeling?
qa.a: She would have felt terrible leaving Pranav alone, so not letting him down mattered more than the blanket.

qa.q: What else could the friends add to their plan?
qa.a: A short midweek call to play one tricky line for each other, so Saturday isn't the only check.

qa.q: How might Pranav experience the arrangement?
qa.a: Pranav gets a reliable partner and honest feedback on his bouncing bow, which helps him improve.

grounding: Two friends learning violin practise together every Saturday and play for each other, which keeps them going even when they feel lazy.

subtype: Approach: practising with a friend for motivation [Action]
passage: I'm Kavitha, Arohi's sister. Every Saturday at four, Arohi's friend Mehr rings our bell with a violin case on her back. They set up in our front room with the music stands facing each other. First Arohi plays the week's piece while Mehr listens with her arms crossed; then they swap. Afterwards they each say something. I've heard "your bow is shaking" and "that bit was beautiful" in the same breath. Last Saturday it was pouring, and Arohi said at lunch she didn't feel like it. At five to four she was still on the sofa. Then the bell rang. Mehr was dripping wet and grinning. Arohi got up without a word and fetched her violin. I don't know if she felt guilty or happy. Maybe both.

qa.q: What time does Mehr ring the bell?
qa.a: Every Saturday at four.

qa.q: Why might Arohi have got up when the bell rang?
qa.a: She may have felt guilty about making Mehr come through the rain for nothing, and glad to see her.

qa.q: What else could the friends do on very rainy days?
qa.a: Practise over a video call, so the Saturday routine continues without anyone getting soaked.

qa.q: What is the routine like for Mehr?
qa.a: Mehr walks through pouring rain grinning, so the Saturdays clearly matter to her too. 🎻

grounding: A sister watches two friends keep a weekly violin practice together, which gets one of them playing even when she does not feel like it.
